abstract: Hypertension-induced myocardial remodelling encompasses both structural and functional changes in cardiac muscle tissue, such as myocardial hypertrophy, fibrosis, and inflammation. These alterations not only impair the systolic and diastolic functions of the heart but also elevate the risk of cardiovascular events and heart failure. One of the primary contributors to hypertensive cardiomyopathy (HTN-CM) is the over-activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), which subsequently induces myocardial remodeling. Although conventional therapeutic strategies aim to suppress RAAS and slow the progression of heart failure, the primary challenge in treating HTN-CM remains the lack of sensitive and specific biomarkers for early detection of myocardial remodelling. Combined multi-omics analyses, complemented by experimental validation, offer a systematic understanding of the landscape of gene/protein/metabolite expression in HTN-CM, revealing the underlying mechanisms of angiotensin II (Ang II)-induced myocardial remodeling in HTN-CM. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are implicated in sphingolipid metabolic processes and are associated with collagen synthesis and inflammatory responses, collectively contributing to myocardial remodeling in HTN-CM. Proteomic analysis demonstrated that differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) are also involved in inflammatory and fibrotic processes, with associations to sphingolipid signaling pathways, particularly manifested through elevated expression of IL6, COL4A1, FGG, FGB, CREBBP and SPHK2 proteins. Metabolomic profiling further elucidated the increased expression of bioactive sphingolipid metabolites S1P and Sa1P in the myocardium of HTN-CM. Integrative multi-omics analysis revealed that HTN-CM is primarily influenced by the sphingolipid signaling pathway, with additional associations to the HIF-1α and FoxO signaling pathways. Correlation analysis has highlighted strong associations between sphingolipids and genes/proteins related to fibrosis and inflammation, as well as their connection to the HIF-1α and FoxO signalling pathways. Furthermore, certain key indicators were validated through ELISA and Western blot analyses in both plasma and myocardial tissue. In conclusion, the findings of this study suggest that excessive Ang II may induce abnormalities in sphingolipid metabolism, resulting in increased levels of S1P in both circulating and myocardial tissues. This elevation in S1P is implicated in myocardial inflammatory and fibrotic alterations, highlighting its pivotal role in myocardial remodeling. The specific mechanism underlying the sphingolipid signaling pathway in myocardial remodeling may involve downstream biological processes, including oxidative stress and excessive mitochondrial autophagy, mediated by HIF-1α and FoxO. (Beijing, China) (License No. SCXK (JING) 2021–0011) and acclimatized for one week. The rats were maintained at 24 °C under constant humidity conditions with a 12:12 h light-dark cycle, and provided ad libitum access to food and water. After one week of acclimatization, the rats were randomly divided into control group (

19
. After six weeks, the tail blood pressure of the rats in each group was measured. Successful HTN-CM modeling was confirmed if the systolic blood pressure of the rats exceeded 140 mmHg, in conjunction with cardiac ultrasound and histopathological examination of the heart muscle. At the end of the 6th week experiment, the rats were fasted overnight and euthanized using anesthesia by inhalation of isoflurane gas to minimize pain. Subsequently, the abdominal aorta blood and heart were dissected and removed. The heart was divided into two parts: one part was fixed with tissue fixative and subjected to Masson’s staining and HE staining, while the other part was snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C for histological testing and experimental validation. The experimental protocol was approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of the Affiliated Hospital of Shandong University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (No. 2021-105). This study was conducted in compliance with ARRIVE guidelines. This study complied with the Regulations on the Management of Laboratory Animals issued by the National Science and Technology Commission and the Implementing Rules for the Management of Medical Laboratory Animals issued by the Health Commission, as well as the relevant statutes of the Experimental Animal Ethics Committee of the Affiliated Hospital of Shandong University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, and the conditions of the staffing and the equipments were in accordance with the requirements.
Echocardiography
At the end of the 6th week of Ang II injection, rats were anaesthetised with isoflurane gas, and echocardiography was performed using the M5 Vet Veterinary Ultrasound system (Mindray, China). In our study, Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) calculation was performed using M-mode echocardiography. Specifically, the Teichholz formula was used to estimate the left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV) and end-systolic volume (LVESV). This method calculates volumes by measuring the end-diastolic and end-systolic internal diameters in parasternal long-axis views of the left ventricle, then applying specific correction formulas. Left ventricular fractional shortening (LVFS) was determined by measuring the changes in left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (LVEDD) and end-systolic diameter (LVESD). LVEF (%) = (EDV -ESV) / EDV × 100% and LVFS (%) = (LVEDD − LVESD) / LVEDD × 100%

RNA integrity was assessed using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Transcriptome libraries were constructed using the VAHTS Universal V5 RNA-seq Library Prep Kit according to the instructions. Transcriptome sequencing was performed by Shanghai OE Biotech. Co., Ltd. The libraries were sequenced using the Illumina Novaseq 6000 sequencing platform, and 150 bp paired-end reads were generated. The raw reads in fastq format were processed using fastp software, and clean reads were obtained by removing low-quality reads for subsequent data analysis
21
. Reference genome comparison was performed using HISAT2 software
22

23

24
. Principal component analysis (PCA) of genes (counts) as well as mapping was performed using R (v 3.2.0) to assess sample biological replicates. The counts of each sample gene were normalized using DESeq2 software (BaseMean values were utilized to estimate expression)
25
. Subsequently, FC were calculated, and differences were tested for significance using the negative binomial distribution test. The final criteria for screening differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were FC = 2 and
P
< 0.05. Hierarchical clustering analyses of the DEGs were performed to demonstrate the expression patterns of the genes across groups and samples using R. The genes were then analyzed using the hypergeometric distribution algorithm. Subsequently, GO and KEGG (
http://www.kegg.jp/kegg/kegg1.html

Gene set enrichment analyses (GSEA) were performed using GSEA software, which uses predefined gene sets to rank genes according to their degree of differential expression in the two types of samples, and then examines whether a predefined set of genes is enriched at the top or the bottom of this ranked list. The results for all DEGs and pathway analyses were corrected for the false discovery rate (FDR) of P-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. This method adjusts P-values to reduce the risk of false positives associated with multiple testing.
TMT-labelled quantitative proteomic analysis
The frozen sample was removed, liquid nitrogen was added, and it was ground thoroughly. Then, sample lysate, phosphatase inhibitor, and protease inhibitor PMSF were added to a final concentration of 1 mM. Ultrasonic crushing was performed on ice at 80 W. The solution was centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant was collected. The supernatant represented the total protein solution of the samples, and the protein concentration was determined using the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) protein concentration assay method before dispensing and storage at −80 °C. For each sample, 10 µg of protein was taken and separated by 12% SDS-PAGE; the separated gel was stained with Coomassie Blue using the eStain LG Protein Stainer. The stained gel was imaged using a fully automated digital gel image analysis system. According to the determined protein concentration, 50 µg of protein was taken from each sample, and the different groups of samples were diluted and adjusted to the same concentration and volume with lysis solution. Dithiothreitol (DTT) was added to the protein solution at a final concentration of 5 mM, mixed well, and incubated for 30 min at 55 °C. Cooling was then performed on ice until room temperature was reached. The appropriate volume of iodoacetamide was added to give a final concentration of 10 mM, mixed well, and left at room temperature for 15 min, protected from light. Six times the volume of acetone was added to the solution above to precipitate the proteins, and left at −20 °C for more than 4 h or overnight. The precipitates were then centrifuged for 10 min at 8,000 x g at 4 °C, and the supernatant was discarded. The acetone was evaporated for 2–3 min. 100 µL of TEAB (200 mM) was added to reconstitute the precipitate, adding 1/50th of the sample mass, and then adding 1/50th of the sample mass to the precipitate. 100 µL of TEAB (200 mM) was added to redissolve the precipitate, and 1/50th of the sample mass of 1 mg/mL Trypsin-TPCK was added, and digestion was carried out overnight at 37 °C. The digested samples were lyophilized and stored at −80 °C. The lyophilized samples were reconstituted with 100 mM TEAB buffer, mixed well with shaking, and the labeling reaction was performed in a 1.5 mL Eppendorf tube.
The Tandem Mass Tags (TMT) reagent was removed from the refrigerator and allowed to equilibrate to room temperature. The reagent was reconstituted by adding anhydrous acetonitrile, then shaken and centrifuged. The TMT reagent was added to the sample, ensuring thorough mixing, and left at room temperature for 1 h. The reaction was terminated by adding 5% hydroxylamine, then the mixture was lyophilized and stored at −80 °C. For reverse chromatographic separation using liquid chromatography (Agilent 1100 HPLC), the Agilent Zorbax Extend - C18 narrow column, 2.1 × 150 mm, with a particle size of 5 μm, was employed. The detection wavelength was set to UV 210 nm. Mobile phase A consisted of ACN-H2O (2:98, v/v), with pH adjusted to 10 using ammonia, while mobile phase B comprised ACN-H2O (90:10, v/v), also with pH adjusted to 10 using ammonia. The flow rate was maintained at 300 µL/min. The gradient elution conditions were as follows: 0–8 min, 98% A; 8–8.01 min, 98–95% A; 8.01–30 min, 95–80% A; 30–43 min, 80 − 65% A; 43–53 min, 65 − 55% A. Specifically, at 53 min, the gradient changed from 65–55% A; at 53–53.01 min, it transitioned from 55% A to 10% A; at 53.01–63 min, it remained at 10% A; at 63–63.01 min, it changed from 10% A to 98% A; finally, from 63.01 to 68 min, it stabilized at 98% A. Samples were collected over the 8–54 min timeframe. The eluent was collected into sequentially numbered centrifuge tubes at one-minute intervals, starting from tubes 1 to 15, and then the sequence 1→15 was repeated.
After collection, the sample was evaporated to dryness and then stored frozen for mass spectrometry. Concerning chromatographic conditions, the samples were loaded at a flow rate of 300 nL/min and separated using an Acclaim PepMap RSLC column, sized 75 μm × 50 cm (RP-C18, Thermo Fisher). For the mobile phases, mobile phase A comprised ACN-H
2
O-FA (99.9:0.1, v/v), while mobile phase B consisted of ACN-H

O-FA (80:19.9:0.1, v/v/v). The gradient elution conditions were as follows: 0 to 50 min, 2–28% B; 50 to 60 min, 28–42% B; 60 to 65 min, 42–90% B. Regarding MS conditions, the primary MS mass resolution was set to 45,000, the automatic gain control value was set to 3e6, and the maximum injection time was 30 ms. The MS scan covered a full-scan charge-to-mass ratio m/z range of 350–1500, and MS/MS scans were performed on the 20 highest peaks. All MS/MS pattern acquisitions were conducted using data-dependent positive-ion mode. Additionally, all MS/MS spectra were obtained using high-energy collisional cleavage in data-dependent positive-ion mode, with the collision energy set to 32. The resolution of MS/MS was set to 3000, the automatic gain control was set to 2e5, and the maximum ion injection time was set to 40 ms. The dynamic exclusion time was set to 30 s.
The data were analyzed using ProteomeDiscoverer 2.4.1.15 (ThermoFisher Scientific). P
< 0.05. GO and KEGG Pathway enrichment analyses were conducted on DEPs using the hypergeometric distribution algorithm to identify significantly enriched functional entries. The DEPs were analyzed in the STRING database to obtain the interaction relationships.
Full spectrum metabolism—dual platform metabolomics analysis
The analytical instruments used in this experiment were the Waters ACQUITY UPLC I-Class Plus/Thermo QE ultra-high performance liquid tandem high-resolution mass spectrometer and the Agilent 7890B-5977 A gas chromatograph equipped with a mass spectrometry platform system. A 30 mg sample was weighed into a 1.5 mL centrifuge tube, and two small steel beads along with 600 µL of methanol-water (V = 4:1 with mixed internal standard, 4 µg/mL) were added. After refrigerating at −40 °C for 2 min, the sample was ground (60 Hz, 2 min) and extracted using ultrasound for 10 min in an ice-water bath. Subsequently, it was allowed to stand overnight at −40 °C and then centrifuged at low temperature (12,000 rpm, 4 °C) for 10 min. 150 µL of supernatant was aspirated with a syringe, filtered using a 0.22 μm organic-phase pore filter, transferred to an LC injection vial, and stored at −80 °C until LC-MS analysis. Simultaneously, 150 µL of supernatant was loaded into a glass derivatization vial, and the sample was dried using a centrifugal concentrator. 80 µL of pyridine methoxylamine hydrochloride solution was added to the glass derivatization vial, and the sample was dried. The samples were then removed from the derivatization vials, and 50 µL of BSTFA derivatization reagent and 20 µL of hexane were added to the glass derivatization vials, along with 10 µL of 10 internal standards (C8/C9/C10/C12/C14/C16/C18/C20/C22/C24 in chloroform). The mixture was reacted at 70 °C for 60 min. After removing the samples, they were left at room temperature for 30 min for GC-MS metabolomics analysis. Quality control (QC) samples were prepared by mixing the extracts of all samples in equal volumes.
Chromatographic conditions: LC: Column: ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 (100 mm × 2.1 mm, 1.8 μm); Column temperature: 45 ℃; Mobile phase: A-water (containing 0.1% formic acid), B-acetonitrile; Flow rate: 0.35 mL/min; Injection volume: 3 µL; GC: DB-5MS capillary column (30 m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 μm, Agilent J&W Scientific, Folsom, CA, USA), carrier gas was high-purity helium (purity less than 99.999%), flow rate: 1.0 mL/min; injection volume: 3 µL. The carrier gas was high-purity helium (purity not less than 99.999%), the flow rate was 1.0 mL/min, and the temperature of the inlet port was 260 °C. The injection volume was 1 µL, and the injection was performed without split flow. Programmed temperature increase: the initial temperature of the column oven was 60 °C, held for 0.5 min; the temperature was programmed to increase to 125 °C at 8 °C/min; 210 °C at 8 °C/min; 270 °C at 15 °C/min; and 305 °C at 20 °C/min, and held for 5 min. Mass spectrometry conditions-LC-MS/MS: Ion source: ESI; Sample mass spectra Signal acquisition was carried out separately for positive and negative ions, and the specific acquisition mode was DDA (data dependent acquisition). Mass spectrometry conditions-GC-MS: electron bombardment ion source (EI), ion source temperature 230 °C, quadrupole temperature 150 °C, electron energy 70 eV. Scanning mode is full scan mode (SCAN), mass scanning range: m/z 50–500. The pre-treatment, derivatisation, sample on-boarding and mass spectrometry system stability were analysed and evaluated through the quality control of the internal standard and QC samples in the experimental part of the project. Stability was analysed and evaluated.
Prior to pattern recognition, raw data underwent baseline filtering, peak identification, integration, retention time correction, peak alignment, and normalization using the metabolomics processing software Progenesis QI v3.0 (Nonlinear Dynamics, Newcastle, UK). Qualitative and quantitative analyses of small molecule mass deconvolution were conducted using MS-DIAL on gas data collected in Full Scan mode. Compound identification, based on multiple dimensions such as retention time (RT), exact mass number, secondary fragmentation, and isotopic distribution, was performed using The Human Metabolome Database (HMDB), Lipidmaps (v2.3), and METLIN databases, along with the LuMet-Animal local database. Orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) was utilized to differentiate the overall differences in metabolic profiles between groups and identify differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs). To avoid overfitting, a seven-fold cyclic cross-validation and 200 times response permutation testing (RPT) were employed to assess the model’s quality. Comparative metabolic difference analyses were conducted using both multivariate and univariate statistical methods. Following DEMs screening, metabolic pathway enrichment analysis was performed on DEMs based on the KEGG database. Finally, a weighted co-expression network model was constructed based on selected power values.
Multi-omics joint analysis
Initially, DEGs, DEPs, and DEMs were concurrently mapped to the KEGG pathway database to obtain their shared pathway information. The pathway with the lowest P-value and the highest number of differential expressions was deemed the key pathway. Additionally, correlation coefficients between all data entries of DEGs, DEPs, and DEMs were computed using the Pearson correlation algorithm. Subsequently, the DEGs-DEPs-DEMs correlation network was established using Cytoscape for pairs of correlations with
P
< 0.05.
HE and Masson histological staining
The tissue was removed from the fixative, dehydrated, and then immersed in wax. Subsequently, the wax-impregnated tissues were embedded using an embedding machine. The trimmed wax blocks were sliced to a thickness of 4 μm using a paraffin slicer. The resulting paraffin slices were dewaxed to water, followed by staining with hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) (Cat No. G1076, Servicebio, China) and Masson stain (Cat No. G1006, Servicebio, China) to observe the morphology of myocardial cells, inflammation cell infiltration, and the degree of fibrosis, respectively. H&E staining revealed blue nuclei and red cytoplasm, while Masson staining displayed blue collagen fibers; myofibrils, fibrils, and erythrocytes appeared red. Sections stained with H&E and Masson were examined using a Nikon Eclipse E100 normal light microscope (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan). Images were captured using CaseViewer software, and the fraction of blue area representing collagen fibers was quantified using ImageJ software (NIH, USA).
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
S1P and N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels were quantified in serum or myocardial tissue using ELISA kits [S1P (Cat No. JYM1296Ra, Gene Beauty, Wuhan, China), NT-proBNP (Cat No. JYM0213Ra, Gene Beauty, Wuhan, China)]. All experimental procedures strictly adhered to the instructions provided with the ELISA kits.
Western blot
Myocardial tissue (50 mg) was lysed in Radio Immunoprecipitation Assay (RIPA) Lysis Buffer (Cat No. P0013B, Beyotime, China) to extract proteins, and the protein concentration was adjusted to 2 µg/µL using the BCA kit (Cat No. CW0014S, Cwbio, Jiangsu, China) for assessment. Next, a One-Step PAGE Gel Rapid Preparation Kit (10%) (Cat No. E303-01, Vazyme, Nanjing, China) was used to isolate 15 µL of diluted proteins. The proteins were then transferred to a PVDF membrane (Cat No. WGPVDF45, Millipore, Massachusetts, USA) for immunoblotting. Subsequently, the membrane was incubated in 5% skimmed milk at 25 °C for 1 h. Then, the membranes were washed and incubated overnight at 4 °C with the following primary antibodies: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) (Cat No. ET1601-4, HUABIO, China), Sphingosine kinase 1 (SPHK1) (Cat No. 10670-1-AP, Proteintech, Wuhan, China), Sphingosine kinase 2 (SPHK2) (Cat No. 21898-1-AP, Proteintech, Wuhan, China), Hypoxia Inducible Factor-1α (HIF-1α) (Cat No. ab179483, Abcam, Cambridge, United Kingdom), Transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) (Cat No. 21898-1-AP, Proteintech, Wuhan, China), Forkhead Box O1 (FOXO1) (Cat No. ET1608-25, HUABIO, China). After washing, the membrane was incubated with a species-specific secondary antibody conjugated to HRP. The SuperPico ECL Chemiluminescence Kit (Cat No. E422-01, Vazyme, Nanjing, China) was used to visualize the protein bands. Finally, the protein content was analyzed by densitometric quantification using the Tanon 5200 Fully Automated Chemiluminescent Image Analysis System (Tanon, Shanghai, China).
Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (v 9) and RStudio. The results were presented as mean ± SD. Univariate statistical analysis was conducted using Student’s t-test to evaluate statistical significance, with
p
< 0.05 considered as indicative of statistical significance.

Introduction
Hypertension is a major health problem worldwide, and the cardiac effects of hypertension go beyond a mere increase in blood pressure; it is considered one of the major risk factors for myocardial remodelling and heart failure (HF)
1
,
2
. Hypertensive cardiomyopathy (HTN-CM) is the most common complication caused by prolonged hypertension, which is mainly characterised by left ventricular hypertrophy and myocardial remodelling
3
,
4
. As the disease progresses, these pathological changes can eventually lead to HF
5
. Specific plasma proteins are thought to play an important role in mediating the effects of hypertension on cardiac structure and function
2
. This suggests that even when blood pressure is well controlled, it may not be possible to completely prevent or reverse cardiac remodelling caused by hypertension, emphasising the importance of early diagnosis and intervention. Although many studies have revealed the pathophysiological mechanisms of hypertension-induced cardiomyopathy, the exact molecular mechanisms remain incompletely elucidated, and sensitive and specific biomarkers for early detection of myocardial remodelling are still lacking
6
. Addressing HTN-CM poses a significant challenge to the cardiovascular field, necessitating efforts to impede or delay the disease progression, reduce adverse events, and improve patients’ quality of life.
Pathological cardiac remodelling is commonly associated with inflammation, fibrosis, and cellular dysfunction, such as abnormal interactions between cardiomyocytes and non-cardiomyocytes, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, disrupted autophagy, and impaired metabolic and signalling pathways
7
. Myocardial fibrosis constitutes a key aspect of the pathological remodeling response and is defined by the accumulation of excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins, including collagen and fibronectin, during the progression of myocardial injury or inflammatory diseases stemming from various causes
8
,
9
. Type I and III protofibrillar collagens (COL1 and 3) serve as the primary constituents of the ECM, accounting for approximately 80% and 10%, respectively, of the collagen in the healthy heart. While the former provides tensile strength, the latter maintains the elasticity of the matrix network
10
,
11
. In addition, the inflammatory response plays a key role in cardiac repair, not only by removing dead cells and debris but also by activating essential pathways for scar formation
12
. It is widely acknowledged that inflammation can foster the development of diverse fibrotic processes. In HTN-CM, the infiltration and activation of inflammatory cells, such as macrophages and T lymphocytes, in myocardial tissues promote apoptosis and myocardial fibrosis, thus contributing to myocardial remodelling. Inflammatory cells release a variety of inflammatory mediators, including tumour necrosis factor α (TNF-α), interleukin 1β (IL-1β), and interleukin 6 (IL-6). These mediators further activate cardiomyocytes and fibroblasts, increase oxidative stress in cardiomyocytes, and promote myocardial fibrosis
13
. Inflammation, collagen deposition, and fibrosis play pivotal roles in the augmentation and progression of adverse cardiac remodeling in HTN-CM; thus, targeting myocardial inflammatory-fibrotic alterations emerges as a crucial strategy for managing cardiac remodeling in HTN-CM.
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is regarded as one of the most potent regulators of sodium homeostasis, fluid volume, and blood pressure within the body
14
. Angiotensin II (Ang II) and aldosterone represent two of the most potent biologically active products of the RAAS, and elevated circulating and tissue levels of Ang II and aldosterone precipitate a pro-fibrotic, inflammatory, and hypertrophic environment, contributing to cardiac remodeling and dysfunction
15
,
16
. An exaggerated inflammatory response stands out as a key characteristic of RAAS-mediated cardiac remodeling
17
. However, there remains a necessity for further exploration into medications targeting the intermediary processes linking Ang II and inflammation-fibrosis. While it is widely acknowledged that Ang II is intricately linked to cardiac remodeling, the precise mechanisms through which Ang II influences the inflammatory and fibrotic processes in the heart remain incompletely understood.
The advent of multi-omics technology heralds the era of big data in life sciences. This evolutionary trajectory has become inevitable, as it not only facilitates a comprehensive elucidation of the overall landscape of diseases but also enables a profound exploration of their underlying molecular mechanisms. Clinical investigations into HTN-CM have thus far primarily focused on preliminary biomarker screening from patient plasma, owing to the challenges associated with acquiring myocardial tissue, necessitating further validation
2
. However, to date, no study has examined HTN-CM using a multi-omics approach. This study demonstrates that Ang II stress induces disruption of sphingolipid metabolism and activates sphingosine kinase (SPHK), increasing sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) levels, thereby triggering inflammation and myocardial fibrosis, subsequently affecting myocardial remodeling. Additionally, excessive S1P may exert further effects on the HIF-1α and FoxO signaling pathways. Figure

The results for all DEGs and pathway analyses were corrected for the false discovery rate (FDR) of P-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. This method adjusts P-values to reduce the risk of false positives associated with multiple testing.
TMT-labelled quantitative proteomic analysis
The frozen sample was removed, liquid nitrogen was added, and it was ground thoroughly. Then, sample lysate, phosphatase inhibitor, and protease inhibitor PMSF were added to a final concentration of 1 mM. Ultrasonic crushing was performed on ice at 80 W. The solution was centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant was collected. The supernatant represented the total protein solution of the samples, and the protein concentration was determined using the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) protein concentration assay method before dispensing and storage at −80 °C. For each sample, 10 µg of protein was taken and separated by 12% SDS-PAGE; the separated gel was stained with Coomassie Blue using the eStain LG Protein Stainer. The stained gel was imaged using a fully automated digital gel image analysis system. According to the determined protein concentration, 50 µg of protein was taken from each sample, and the different groups of samples were diluted and adjusted to the same concentration and volume with lysis solution. Dithiothreitol (DTT) was added to the protein solution at a final concentration of 5 mM, mixed well, and incubated for 30 min at 55 °C. Cooling was then performed on ice until room temperature was reached. The appropriate volume of iodoacetamide was added to give a final concentration of 10 mM, mixed well, and left at room temperature for 15 min, protected from light. Six times the volume of acetone was added to the solution above to precipitate the proteins, and left at −20 °C for more than 4 h or overnight. The precipitates were then centrifuged for 10 min at 8,000 x g at 4 °C, and the supernatant was discarded. The acetone was evaporated for 2–3 min. 100 µL of TEAB (200 mM) was added to reconstitute the precipitate, adding 1/50th of the sample mass, and then adding 1/50th of the sample mass to the precipitate. 100 µL of TEAB (200 mM) was added to redissolve the precipitate, and 1/50th of the sample mass of 1 mg/mL Trypsin-TPCK was added, and digestion was carried out overnight at 37 °C. The digested samples were lyophilized and stored at −80 °C. The lyophilized samples were reconstituted with 100 mM TEAB buffer, mixed well with shaking, and the labeling reaction was performed in a 1.5 mL Eppendorf tube.
The Tandem Mass Tags (TMT) reagent was removed from the refrigerator and allowed to equilibrate to room temperature. The reagent was reconstituted by adding anhydrous acetonitrile, then shaken and centrifuged. The TMT reagent was added to the sample, ensuring thorough mixing, and left at room temperature for 1 h. The reaction was terminated by adding 5% hydroxylamine, then the mixture was lyophilized and stored at −80 °C. For reverse chromatographic separation using liquid chromatography (Agilent 1100 HPLC), the Agilent Zorbax Extend - C18 narrow column, 2.1 × 150 mm, with a particle size of 5 μm, was employed. The detection wavelength was set to UV 210 nm. Mobile phase A consisted of ACN-H2O (2:98, v/v), with pH adjusted to 10 using ammonia, while mobile phase B comprised ACN-H2O (90:10, v/v), also with pH adjusted to 10 using ammonia. The flow rate was maintained at 300 µL/min. The gradient elution conditions were as follows: 0–8 min, 98% A; 8–8.01 min, 98–95% A; 8.01–30 min, 95–80% A; 30–43 min, 80 − 65% A; 43–53 min, 65 − 55% A. Specifically, at 53 min, the gradient changed from 65–55% A; at 53–53.01 min, it transitioned from 55% A to 10% A; at 53.01–63 min, it remained at 10% A; at 63–63.01 min, it changed from 10% A to 98% A; finally, from 63.01 to 68 min, it stabilized at 98% A. Samples were collected over the 8–54 min timeframe. The eluent was collected into sequentially numbered centrifuge tubes at one-minute intervals, starting from tubes 1 to 15, and then the sequence 1→15 was repeated.
After collection, the sample was evaporated to dryness and then stored frozen for mass spectrometry. Concerning chromatographic conditions, the samples were loaded at a flow rate of 300 nL/min and separated using an Acclaim PepMap RSLC column, sized 75 μm × 50 cm (RP-C18, Thermo Fisher). For the mobile phases, mobile phase A comprised ACN-H
2
O-FA (99.9:0.1, v/v), while mobile phase B consisted of ACN-H
2
O-FA (80:19.9:0.1, v/v/v). The gradient elution conditions were as follows: 0 to 50 min, 2–28% B; 50 to 60 min, 28–42% B; 60 to 65 min, 42–90% B. Regarding MS conditions, the primary MS mass resolution was set to 45,000, the automatic gain control value was set to 3e6, and the maximum injection time was 30 ms. The MS scan covered a full-scan charge-to-mass ratio m/z range of 350–1500, and MS/MS scans were performed on the 20 highest peaks. All MS/MS pattern acquisitions were conducted using data-dependent positive-ion mode. Additionally, all MS/MS spectra were obtained using high-energy collisional cleavage in data-dependent positive-ion mode, with the collision energy set to 32. The resolution of MS/MS was set to 3000, the automatic gain control was set to 2e5, and the maximum ion injection time was set to 40 ms. The dynamic exclusion time was set to 30 s.
The data were analyzed using ProteomeDiscoverer 2.4.1.15 (ThermoFisher Scientific). After obtaining the raw data from the database search, proteins with Score Sequest HT > 0, unique peptide ≥ 1, and non-null expression values were screened. The median of the screened proteins was normalized and log2 transformed to obtain the plausible proteins. PCA was performed using the expression of plausible proteins, and differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were screened with FC ≥ 1.2 or FC ≤ 0.83 and
P
< 0.05. GO and KEGG Pathway enrichment analyses were conducted on DEPs using the hypergeometric distribution algorithm to identify significantly enriched functional entries. The DEPs were analyzed in the STRING database to obtain the interaction relationships.
Full spectrum metabolism—dual platform metabolomics analysis
The analytical instruments used in this experiment were the Waters ACQUITY UPLC I-Class Plus/Thermo QE ultra-high performance liquid tandem high-resolution mass spectrometer and the Agilent 7890B-5977 A gas chromatograph equipped with a mass spectrometry platform system. A 30 mg sample was weighed into a 1.5 mL centrifuge tube, and two small steel beads along with 600 µL of methanol-water (V = 4:1 with mixed internal standard, 4 µg/mL) were added. After refrigerating at −40 °C for 2 min, the sample was ground (60 Hz, 2 min) and extracted using ultrasound for 10 min in an ice-water bath. Subsequently, it was allowed to stand overnight at −40 °C and then centrifuged at low temperature (12,000 rpm, 4 °C) for 10 min. 150 µL of supernatant was aspirated with a syringe, filtered using a 0.22 μm organic-phase pore filter, transferred to an LC injection vial, and stored at −80 °C until LC-MS analysis. Simultaneously, 150 µL of supernatant was loaded into a glass derivatization vial, and the sample was dried using a centrifugal concentrator. 80 µL of pyridine methoxylamine hydrochloride solution was added to the glass derivatization vial, and the sample was dried. The samples were then removed from the derivatization vials, and 50 µL of BSTFA derivatization reagent and 20 µL of hexane were added to the glass derivatization vials, along with 10 µL of 10 internal standards (C8/C9/C10/C12/C14/C16/C18/C20/C22/C24 in chloroform). The mixture was reacted at 70 °C for 60 min. After removing the samples, they were left at room temperature for 30 min for GC-MS metabolomics analysis. Quality control (QC) samples were prepared by mixing the extracts of all samples in equal volumes.
Chromatographic conditions: LC: Column: ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 (100 mm × 2.1 mm, 1.8 μm); Column temperature: 45 ℃; Mobile phase: A-water (containing 0.1% formic acid), B-acetonitrile; Flow rate: 0.35 mL/min; Injection volume: 3 µL; GC: DB-5MS capillary column (30 m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 μm, Agilent J&W Scientific, Folsom, CA, USA), carrier gas was high-purity helium (purity less than 99.999%), flow rate: 1.0 mL/min; injection volume: 3 µL. The carrier gas was high-purity helium (purity not less than 99.999%), the flow rate was 1.0 mL/min, and the temperature of the inlet port was 260 °C. The injection volume was 1 µL, and the injection was performed without split flow. Programmed temperature increase: the initial temperature of the column oven was 60 °C, held for 0.5 min; the temperature was programmed to increase to 125 °C at 8 °C/min; 210 °C at 8 °C/min; 270 °C at 15 °C/min; and 305 °C at 20 °C/min, and held for 5 min. Mass spectrometry conditions-LC-MS/MS: Ion source: ESI; Sample mass spectra Signal acquisition was carried out separately for positive and negative ions, and the specific acquisition mode was DDA (data dependent acquisition). Mass spectrometry conditions-GC-MS: electron bombardment ion source (EI), ion source temperature 230 °C, quadrupole temperature 150 °C, electron energy 70 eV. Scanning mode is full scan mode (SCAN), mass scanning range: m/z 50–500. The pre-treatment, derivatisation, sample on-boarding and mass spectrometry system stability were analysed and evaluated through the quality control of the internal standard and QC samples in the experimental part of the project. Stability was analysed and evaluated.
Prior to pattern recognition, raw data underwent baseline filtering, peak identification, integration, retention time correction, peak alignment, and normalization using the metabolomics processing software Progenesis QI v3.0 (Nonlinear Dynamics, Newcastle, UK). Qualitative and quantitative analyses of small molecule mass deconvolution were conducted using MS-DIAL on gas data collected in Full Scan mode. Compound identification, based on multiple dimensions such as retention time (RT), exact mass number, secondary fragmentation, and isotopic distribution, was performed using The Human Metabolome Database (HMDB), Lipidmaps (v2.3), and METLIN databases, along with the LuMet-Animal local database. Orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) was utilized to differentiate the overall differences in metabolic profiles between groups and identify differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs). To avoid overfitting, a seven-fold cyclic cross-validation and 200 times response permutation testing (RPT) were employed to assess the model’s quality. Comparative metabolic difference analyses were conducted using both multivariate and univariate statistical methods. Following DEMs screening, metabolic pathway enrichment analysis was performed on DEMs based on the KEGG database. Finally, a weighted co-expression network model was constructed based on selected power values.
Multi-omics joint analysis
Initially, DEGs, DEPs, and DEMs were concurrently mapped to the KEGG pathway database to obtain their shared pathway information. The pathway with the lowest P-value and the highest number of differential expressions was deemed the key pathway. Additionally, correlation coefficients between all data entries of DEGs, DEPs, and DEMs were computed using the Pearson correlation algorithm. Subsequently, the DEGs-DEPs-DEMs correlation network was established using Cytoscape for pairs of correlations with
P
< 0.05.
HE and Masson histological staining
The tissue was removed from the fixative, dehydrated, and then immersed in wax. Subsequently, the wax-impregnated tissues were embedded using an embedding machine. The trimmed wax blocks were sliced to a thickness of 4 μm using a paraffin slicer. The resulting paraffin slices were dewaxed to water, followed by staining with hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) (Cat No. G1076, Servicebio, China) and Masson stain (Cat No. G1006, Servicebio, China) to observe the morphology of myocardial cells, inflammation cell infiltration, and the degree of fibrosis, respectively. H&E staining revealed blue nuclei and red cytoplasm, while Masson staining displayed blue collagen fibers; myofibrils, fibrils, and erythrocytes appeared red. Sections stained with H&E and Masson were examined using a Nikon Eclipse E100 normal light microscope (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan). Images were captured using CaseViewer software, and the fraction of blue area representing collagen fibers was quantified using ImageJ software (NIH, USA).
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
S1P and N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels were quantified in serum or myocardial tissue using ELISA kits [S1P (Cat No. JYM1296Ra, Gene Beauty, Wuhan, China), NT-proBNP (Cat No. JYM0213Ra, Gene Beauty, Wuhan, China)]. All experimental procedures strictly adhered to the instructions provided with the ELISA kits.
Western blot
Myocardial tissue (50 mg) was lysed in Radio Immunoprecipitation Assay (RIPA) Lysis Buffer (Cat No. P0013B, Beyotime, China) to extract proteins, and the protein concentration was adjusted to 2 µg/µL using the BCA kit (Cat No. CW0014S, Cwbio, Jiangsu, China) for assessment. Next, a One-Step PAGE Gel Rapid Preparation Kit (10%) (Cat No. E303-01, Vazyme, Nanjing, China) was used to isolate 15 µL of diluted proteins. The proteins were then transferred to a PVDF membrane (Cat No. WGPVDF45, Millipore, Massachusetts, USA) for immunoblotting. Subsequently, the membrane was incubated in 5% skimmed milk at 25 °C for 1 h. Then, the membranes were washed and incubated overnight at 4 °C with the following primary antibodies: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) (Cat No. ET1601-4, HUABIO, China), Sphingosine kinase 1 (SPHK1) (Cat No. 10670-1-AP, Proteintech, Wuhan, China), Sphingosine kinase 2 (SPHK2) (Cat No. 21898-1-AP, Proteintech, Wuhan, China), Hypoxia Inducible Factor-1α (HIF-1α) (Cat No. ab179483, Abcam, Cambridge, United Kingdom), Transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) (Cat No. 21898-1-AP, Proteintech, Wuhan, China), Forkhead Box O1 (FOXO1) (Cat No. ET1608-25, HUABIO, China). After washing, the membrane was incubated with a species-specific secondary antibody conjugated to HRP. The SuperPico ECL Chemiluminescence Kit (Cat No. E422-01, Vazyme, Nanjing, China) was used to visualize the protein bands. Finally, the protein content was analyzed by densitometric quantification using the Tanon 5200 Fully Automated Chemiluminescent Image Analysis System (Tanon, Shanghai, China).
Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (v 9) and RStudio. The results were presented as mean ± SD. Univariate statistical analysis was conducted using Student’s t-test to evaluate statistical significance, with
p
< 0.05 considered as indicative of statistical significance.

. Furthermore, systemic inflammation promotes the transformation of fibroblasts into activated myofibroblasts through the secretion of TGF-β
30
. These myofibroblasts deposit collagen, contributing to cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation, which in turn exacerbates ventricular stiffness and diastolic dysfunction
31
,
32
. Although cardiac hypertrophy and hypertension may persist, the prognosis of HTN-CM largely depends on the improvement of fibrosis and inflammation
31
,
32
. Consequently, the inhibition of myocardial remodelling through the reversal of inflammatory responses and fibrotic changes presents a promising therapeutic strategy for managing HTN-CM.
This study is the first to combine transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics to analyze the molecular mechanisms of Ang II-induced myocardial remodeling in HTN-CM. The co-analysis of this study identified Sphingolipid metabolism, the Sphingolipid signaling pathway, the HIF-1 signaling pathway, and the FoxO signaling pathway as the key pathways of interest. Correlation analysis also indicated that S1P and Sa1P were associated with inflammatory-fibrotic genes/proteins in the transcriptome and proteome, predominantly influenced by the Sphingolipid signaling pathway, and correlated with the HIF-1 signaling pathway and FoxO signaling pathway.
Ang II is known to promote cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, fibrosis, and cardiac remodeling by binding to its type 1 receptor (AT1R). Activation of AT1R increases sodium retention, vasoconstriction, and enhances sympathetic nervous system activity, all of which contribute to cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, fibrosis, and cardiac remodeling
33
,
34
. In HTN-CM, collagen metabolism is significantly disrupted. Specifically, the balance between the synthesis and degradation of type I and type III collagen molecules is disturbed, leading to excessive accumulation of collagen fibres in the myocardial interstitial space and perivascular space
35
. In our study, we also found elevated mRNA and protein levels of Collagen IV(Col4) in myocardial tissues affected by HTN-CM. Increased myocardial thickening is usually associated with an increase in Col4, beyond just fibrillar collagen. Col4 plays a key role in the disruption of the cardiomyocyte basement membrane and is closely associated with cardiac remodelling and fibrosis
36
. The basement membrane is a specialised extracellular matrix composed of collagen, laminin, and proteoglycans such as perlecan and nidogens
37
. Disruption of the basement membrane ultimately contributes to the development of myocardial fibrosis by altering the structure and function of the cardiac ECM, promoting inflammation and fibrosis, and affecting the behaviour and interactions of cardiac cells. Together, these processes exacerbate the severity and complexity of HTN-CM
38
–
40
. Additionally, there is further evidence that Ang II may affect cardiac remodeling through the HIF-1α signaling pathway, which plays a key role in hypoxic response and energy metabolism, and its role in cardiac remodeling may be related to Ang II
41
. The HIF-1α signaling pathway was also enriched in focus in our findings. The above studies suggest that elevated Ang II plays a key role in the development of myocardial fibrosis in HTN-CM and may be a target for future therapeutic strategies. However, the exact impact of elevated Ang II on HTN-CM and the underlying molecular mechanisms still need to be elucidated by further studies. In our study, we found for the first time that Ang II intervention resulted in elevated S1P and activation of the SPHK/S1P/S1PR pathway in HTN-CM myocardial tissue.
Sphingolipids are integral constituents of cell membranes, crucial for the formation of membrane microdomains. Apart from their structural role, sphingolipids function as signalling molecules, regulating cellular processes such as apoptosis, cell proliferation, and autophagy
42
. S1P, a bioactive lipid molecule within the sphingolipid class, serves as both an intracellular second messenger and an intercellular signalling molecule, modulating diverse biological processes. Synthesized from ceramides by intracellular synthases, S1P is generated via the phosphorylation of sphingomyelin by SPHKs, subsequently released outside the cell through specific transport proteins. Upon release, S1P binds to its specific G-protein-coupled receptors (S1PRs), initiating downstream signalling pathways
43
–
45
. Sa1P, an isomer of S1P, shares a similar molecular structure. Given the minor structural differences between them, there may be overlap or similarity in their metabolic pathways and biological functions. Notably, our study observed elevations in both S1P and Sa1P following Ang II injection. Ang II plays a pivotal role in regulating vascular tone and blood pressure, partly through modulating Ca
2+
mobilization. Previous studies have implicated the involvement of the SPHK1/S1P signalling pathway in Ang II-induced intracellular Ca
2+
mobilization
46
. In vascular smooth muscle cells, Ang II stimulation activates endogenous SPHK1, leading to increased S1P production
46
. These findings suggest that Ang II may contribute to hypertension, inflammation, and myocardial fibrosis by activating SPHK, thereby elevating S1P expression. Our study further corroborated the activation of the S1P signalling pathway by Ang II, particularly by verifying the elevated expression of SPHK1, SPHK2, S1P, and S1PR in HTN-CM.
Activation of the S1P signaling pathway, particularly through the SPHK1/S1P/S1PR signaling axis, has been demonstrated to contribute to various fibrotic diseases, including pulmonary fibrosis, renal fibrosis, and pancreatic fibrosis

. S1P influences the recruitment of inflammatory cells, such as lymphocytes and monocytes, through its receptor S1PRs. The release of these cells and inflammatory factors, such as IL-6, plays a pivotal role

. However, previous evidence regarding the direct or indirect impact of S1P on HTN-CM myocardial fibrosis is lacking. S1P metabolism is modulated at fibrotic lesions by various pro-fibrotic mediators, particularly through interactions with TGF-β, which finely regulates fibrosis development

. In this study, TGF-β1 expression was elevated, and the TGF-β signalling pathway was significantly activated in the model group compared to the control group. Elevated S1P levels were associated with the inflammatory and fibrotic processes in HTN-CM. These mechanisms suggest that the S1P signaling pathway may play a significant role in inflammation and fibrosis in HTN-CM by influencing the expression of TGF-β1 molecules. TGF-β1 is an early marker of inflammation in HTN-CM and may subsequently influence the expression of S1P, which is involved in myocardial fibrosis

–

. However, the specific molecular mechanisms and therapeutic potentials require further investigation. Notably, the S1P signaling pathway was found to be closely associated with the FoxO signaling pathway and the HIF-1 signaling pathway in the multi-omics joint analysis. Specifically, the process known as ROS-induced ROS release is triggered by high levels of ROS, disrupting excitation-contraction coupling and contributing to cardiac remodeling

,

It is activated under hypoxic conditions, which in turn regulate the expression of a variety of genes associated with cellular adaptation to hypoxia

,

Study strengths and limitations
The strength of this study lies in the unbiased big data approach across different biologic spheres (gene/protein/metabolite), providing evidence for the involvement of sphingolipid metabolism in the molecular mechanisms underlying Ang II-induced myocardial remodeling in HTN-CM. However, this study also possesses certain limitations. It only presents initial findings suggesting an association between the activation of the S1P signaling pathway in circulating and myocardial tissues and HTN-CM myocardial remodeling. Whether this pathway directly or indirectly influences HTN-CM myocardial remodeling requires further investigation. Future studies should aim to establish controlled experiments elucidating the relationship between the S1P signaling pathway and processes such as oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction mediated by the HIF-1 and FoxO signaling pathways.
Conclusion
In summary, the present study enhances our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying Ang II-induced myocardial remodeling in HTN-CM through the combined analysis of transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics. This work presents initial observations on the sphingolipid metabolic pathway, particularly the SPHK/S1P/S1PR signaling axis, in the development of Ang II-induced HTN-CM myocardial remodeling. These findings suggest that excessive Ang II may induce abnormalities in S1P metabolism in circulating and myocardial tissues, thereby playing a crucial role in inflammatory and fibrotic changes in the myocardium. The specific mechanism by which S1P contributes to myocardial remodeling may involve biological processes such as oxidative stress and mitochondrial autophagy mediated by HIF-1α and FoxO.
From a clinical standpoint, this study suggests that reversing myocardial inflammation and fibrosis could potentially ameliorate HTN-CM and improve patient survival. Additionally, this research identifies novel targets that offer valuable insights into the development of future therapeutic strategies for HTN-CM. By modulating the activity of SphK isozymes, therapies could be devised to both facilitate myocardial repair and mitigate fibrotic scarring, thereby presenting new avenues for HTN-CM treatment. Given the involvement of sphingolipid metabolism in cardiac remodeling, S1P emerges as a potential biomarker for the clinical diagnosis of HTN-CM, while targeting the activities of SPHK1 and SPHK2 may represent a promising strategy for HTN-CM treatment.
